nodes.text:
# Analysis

Reads: site-kit, brief-reader
Reads (end): massing, every analysis, drawing-graphics

Measure, never guess. Use only the project's site folder (`site.geojson` and its layers) and the brief's `checklist.md`, opened at the brief's pages it names; for the second run add `massing/massing.geojson`. Never write a site, a place or a number of this project into the skill or a script. Every value carries its source (layer, brief page) or is named as an assumption, and a layer or destination the data lacks is left out and named in `summary.md`. Work in Python, in a metric projection, inside the site polygon only (`pip install -r requirements.txt`: shapely, pyproj, networkx).

**What it measures.** Each measure is one row per value in `metrics.csv` and one map.
- **Uses:** the area and share of the site per land use, from the plots and buildings.
- **Edges:** what the site boundary meets (street, rail, water, built, open land), its length in metres, and how many street or path crossings each stretch has.
- **Green:** the green land and its share, split into wooded, open green and farmland, and the brief's green per resident, if the brief gives residents.
- **Walking reach:** the share of the site within 400 m and 800 m along the street and path network of each destination the data has: stations, green, shops and schools. A destination the data lacks is named in the summary as missing and is not measured.
- **Sealed share:** fully sealed (buildings, streets), partly sealed (paths, squares, pitches) and unsealed, in hectares and as a percentage of the site. The class of each land use goes in `config.json`, marked as an assumption.
- **What to keep:** `keep.geojson`, with the existing buildings inside the site, water, woods, scrub, nature reserves and everything the checklist says must stay that the layers show. Each feature has a `reason` and a `source` (the brief's page). Whatever the checklist names but the layers lack goes in the summary.

**Start from the scripts.** Copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/config.example.json` to `analysis/config.json` and fill it from the checklist, each value with its page. Then run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/measure.py" --proposal <proposal folder> --site <site folder> --config <proposal folder>/analysis/config.json --state today` and `draw.py` with the same arguments. On the second run, `--state design` measures the massing in place of what it covers inside the site, with the same method. Then `compare.py --proposal <proposal folder>` reads every `metrics.csv` in the proposal folder and writes `comparison.csv` (`measure, unit, today, design, change, better`) and `comparison.md`, which says in a few lines where the design improves on today and where it doesn't. Whether higher or lower is better comes from `config.json`.

**What to write.** Everything into `analysis/`: `config.json`, `metrics.csv` (`measure, value, unit, state, source`, with `state` either `today` or `design`), `keep.geojson`, a map per measure as SVG with a PNG next to it, the comparison on the second run, and `summary.md` in three lines: what you measured, the sealed share, and what you are unsure of. The maps take their look from `drawing-graphics/standard.md` if it exists, else black lines on white with greys. Open the maps once before you finish.

# Brief reader

Reads: pdf-to-md

The checklist belongs to the brief, not to one version, so it is written once and reused. If `checklist.md` lies next to the brief's Markdown in the project's `brief/` and is newer than every Markdown there, copy it into `brief-reader/` in the proposal folder you are told, write `summary.md`, and stop.

Otherwise read the brief's Markdown in parts, never all at once: list its headings and page markers (`<!-- page N -->`) with `grep`, then read the pages that hold the task, the programme, the rules, the submission and the jury's criteria. Write `checklist.md` next to the brief, in this order, one line per item, each ending with its source as `(<file> p. N)`:

- `## Numbers`: homes, residents, areas per use, green per resident, phases, and every other figure the design must meet.
- `## Rules`: heights, setbacks, what must stay, what is not wanted.
- `## Drawings and scales`: every drawing asked for, with its scale.
- `## Panels and format`: how many panels, their size and orientation, the texts and their length.
- `## Required content`: a numbered list of every item the brief requires on the panels or in the text, in the brief's words.
- `## What the jury looks for`: the criteria, as the brief states them.
- `## Pages`: each topic above and the pages to open for it, so other skills read only those.

Copy it into `brief-reader/` in the proposal folder. Never invent: what the brief doesn't say is written as "not stated". `summary.md`: three lines, the size of the task in one sentence, the number of required items, and what the brief leaves unclear.

# Narrative

Reads: brief-reader, analysis, climate
Reads (end): everything
Model: opus

This skill runs twice: first it builds the conceptual framework the project grows from, then it writes the text that explains the finished project. Work in the proposal folder you are given and write only into `narrative/`. Read the brief's checklist (`brief-reader/checklist.md`) and `analysis/`; if one is missing, use the brief's Markdown and the site folder, and say so in `summary.md`. Never invent a fact: every claim names its file and, where there is one, the brief's page. Everything about the competition and the place comes from the brief.

**First run: the framework.** It must be memorable and solve a conflict, and it may be bold and abstract. Before drafting, read the brief's description of the place, its history and the people who live and work there, in full. Answer from the brief and the analysis what the project is for, who will use it and what it should say. Draft three stories in words, each with a different character (the site, its users or an abstract theme): its desire, the conflict in its way, and the transformation the design brings. Where no character comes naturally, use concept, angle and object. Develop each draft in a short paragraph: what it does at the largest scale, what parts the project is made of and what holds each together, one doorstep, and how it grows over time. Then judge the three as a jury would and choose the best prospect: the one that holds together at every scale, not the one with the neatest sentence or the most exact number. A draft strong in one dimension only is a runner-up. Check that the chosen one doesn't restate the brief's own plan if the brief shows one, and add a move of your own that can be drawn and counted. Only now read `climate/`, as limits the chosen story must meet, unless the brief makes climate its central question. The other skills design from this, so keep it clear. Write `narrative.md`:

- **Story:** the three answers, the three drafts, each in its short paragraph, the chosen one and why, and its character, desire, conflict and transformation.
- **Title and subtitle:** short and memorable, not a slogan; the subtitle at most about eight words.
- **Idea:** one clear sentence without jargon, a paragraph on why this site asks for it, and your own move.
- **Principles:** three to five, one line each, that the design skills can check (where green runs, how dense, how people move). A principle may set its own target, marked as one.
- **Storyline:** one section per panel, in the number and format the checklist gives: its message in one line, and the drawings that carry it, named by the existing skills that make them.
- **Jury:** each criterion from the checklist and where the storyline answers it, or "open" or "partly open".

**Second run: the text.** Read every `summary.md` and table in the proposal folder. Write `text.md` for the jury, explaining the finished project in sequence: the idea, the concept, how it was built up (structure, programme, buildings, open space, movement, phases) and how it was approached (what the site showed, what was decided and why). Fit it into the brief's headings, length and language where the brief sets them, and put any other text it asks for, such as a short one for publication, in a file of its own. Give each key figure its source file in a footnote, and leave out figures that don't exist. Leave `narrative.md` as it is: the drawings were made from it. If the design has moved away from the framework, tell it in `text.md` and name the gap in `summary.md`.

**After each run**, write `summary.md` in three lines: the title and the idea in one sentence; the number that matters most to the idea, with its source; what you are least sure of.

# Programme

Reads: brief-reader

1. Read the brief checklist written by `brief-reader` in the proposal folder you are told, else the newest one. If it is missing, read the brief's Markdown in the project's `brief/`; if a figure is in neither, ask or say so in `summary.md`.
2. Take from the brief everything it asks to build, and table it:
   - **Homes and households:** the number of homes or the housing floor area, the household mix and unit types, and the residents. Where the brief gives a total but no mix, say so and leave the mix open; never invent shares.
   - **Uses and their areas:** commerce and ground-floor uses, schools and daycares with their capacity and outdoor space, community and sport, and anything else the brief lists, each with its gross floor area and plot.
   - **Shared and productive space:** uses shared by day and night, gardens and urban agriculture, shared amenities, only where the brief asks for them or gives a number.
3. Never invent data: next to every number, its source in the brief (with its page) or the assumption behind it, such as m² per resident. No drawings; text and tables only.
4. Write everything into `programme/` in the proposal folder and nothing outside it:
   - `programme.csv`: `use, area_m2, plot_m2, homes, residents, source`, one row per use, so `massing` can check its floor area against it.
   - `households.csv`: `household, share, homes, source`, if the brief gives a mix.
   - `programme.md`: what the brief asks for in words, and its open questions.
5. Create a `summary.md` of exactly three lines:
   - What you tabled.
   - The one key number that matters (total homes).
   - The one assumption or uncertainty you're highlighting.

# Structure plan

Reads: narrative, climate, programme
Model: opus

Set the urban figure in `structure-plan/` of the proposal folder: neighbourhoods, centres, green, routes and gateways, nothing finer. Take the idea and its numbers from `narrative/`, the corridors from `climate/`, homes per phase and commerce from `programme/` (else the brief), the site from the site folder; name what is missing in `summary.md`. Use `site.geojson` as it is and only report where it disagrees with the brief.

**Design.** Start from what is there: keep, then change, then new. Open gateways where streets, stops and landscape meet the site, and continue them in. Name neighbourhoods by their spatial qualities, never by assumed residents. Put the main centre on the stop and gather the homes around it; local centres take the rest. Give green real extent and roles, and keep climate corridors free. Keep homes out of the climate's loud zones and put commerce there to shield them. Follow the narrative's figure and numbers exactly (how many islands on which side, a width, a distance), or say why the site forbids it.

**Hold the programme.** Each phase holds its homes and its floor area (homes, commerce) under the storey cap with 15 % to spare; where it falls short, enlarge the neighbourhoods before raising density. At least half of the homes lie within a 400 m walk of the stop, or say why not.

**Build.** Copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/design.example.py` to `structure-plan/design.py`: one `F.programme(...)`, then one `F.add(...)` per feature, decisions only. Run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/build.py" <proposal>/structure-plan/design.py --site <site> --proposal <proposal> --climate <climate>` and change `design.py` until `checks.txt` shows no SHORT, in at most four builds. They also warn when the first phase has less of the land than of the homes, a main or local route runs over a kept building or along a foot way, or a water green lies above the ground around it. The scripts check every field, clip to the site, cut routes out of neighbourhoods and measure every area. `scripts/georef.py` places a picture from the brief on the site. Needs `pip install shapely pyproj`.

Features: `neighbourhood` (`phase`, `homes`, `density`, `commerce_m2`), `centre` (`level` main or local, `holds`: the stop, shops, a school), `green` (`roles`), `route` (`level` main, local or landscape) and `gateway`, each with `action` (keep, change, new), `basis` (documented, brief, mapped, hypothesis) and `source`.

**`summary.md`, three lines:** the figure, with the homes and floor area each phase holds against those asked; the share of homes within a 400 m walk of the stop, from `checks.txt`; the hypothesis that matters most and the evidence that would settle it. Write nothing else.

# Art direction

Reads: every drawings (end)
Model: opus

Work in the proposal folder you are given, else the newest in the project's `proposals/`; write only to its `art-direction/`. You judge; you never draw or change another skill's files. Read the summary of each drawing skill, the standard in `drawing-graphics/`, and the project's reference images (where its `CLAUDE.md` says, else `references/`) with the file there that says which images are of which kind. If the proposal folder has side-by-side sheets in `.compare/` (references left, ours right, at one print size), look at each once; else open each drawing's PNG beside the references of its kind. Without references, compare with the standard alone and say so in `summary.md`.

For each drawing, find the largest differences from its references, the ones you see first from across the room: what is drawn and what is left out, the amount of detail, the weight of the figure against the ground, the hierarchy, the labels, how the drawing fills its frame. Turn the largest into at most three fixes per skill, each one its scripts can carry out and you could check, saying what to change and by how much ("draw the street trees as crowns at every scale", "label each centre with its uses, as the references do", "crop to the new district and 100 m around it"), never "make it richer". A fix asks only for what a design layer, the narrative or the standard gives, never for invented data. **What it writes:** `view-N_base.svg` and `.png`, `view-N_depth.png`, `view-N_ids.png` (what each pixel is), `view-N.png` and `render.json` (each prompt and model) when rendered, `view-N_stale.png` for a render whose base a later run redrew otherwise, `views_map.svg` and `.png`, `views.json` (each camera, why it was chosen, its scores), `candidates.csv` (not on a `--views` redraw, which leaves any earlier one as it was), `building_status.csv`, `terrain.csv` if fetched, `assumptions.md`, and `summary.md` in three lines: the views, how many from how many candidates, what you're unsure of. With a massing marked `"standin": true`, or a proposal folder named `test`, the view files and `views_map` start with `TEST_`, the other files keep their names, and the summary says so.

# Plans

Reads: brief-reader, narrative, massing, streets, open-space, mobility, structure-plan, ground-floor, drawing-graphics, panel-layout

Copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/config.example.json` to `plans/config.json` in the proposal folder and fill it from the brief's checklist (where the panels' plan, `panel-layout/layout-plan.json` else `layout.json`, has a frame for a plan, take its `file` name and what its `shows` asks from there; the script draws a framed detail area or site plan at the frame's scale and size itself): the scales of the site plan, the figure-ground and each detail area, whether the site plan shows the storeys, the panel size and margin, and for each detail area the structure plan's centre or neighbourhood it is around (or `phase1`, or a point), with the page of each. Give each detail area its own subject: the first the one the brief names; each further one the district centre or one typical neighbourhood, where the design is densest, never the site's edge, so that no two show the same ground. Read the idea in `narrative/narrative.md` and find the one shape that is the idea, by its name, in a design layer or the site: an area (a green, a corridor) or a line (a valley or an edge: the streets, rail or water it follows), not the places the idea mentions or connects (a square on the strip is not the strip; the centres on a valley are not the valley). Put the narrative's word for it and those names in `idea`; where nothing has the idea as a shape, leave `idea` out. Then run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/plans.py" --proposal <proposal folder> --site <site folder> --config <proposal>/plans/config.json --style <proposal>/drawing-graphics/style.json` (`pip install shapely pyproj numpy pillow`; Chrome or Edge for the PNG). It composites what the design skills wrote: buildings from `massing/`, the street surface from `streets/`, the ground from `open-space/`, stops and hubs from `mobility/`, and in the detail areas only the doors, bike stands, play, bus bays and use labels from `ground-floor/`; a layer that is missing is left out and named in `drawings.json`. If `drawings.json` gives a detail area `overlaps` or `weak` (mostly off the site, or hardly a new building in it), give it another `at` and run once more. If it gives `too_small` (the frame cuts off much of the buildings around its centre), name it in `summary.md` for panel-layout, which owns the frames. A detail area's `not_shown` names what its layers don't give (entrances, play, uses): never draw these yourself, name them in `summary.md` with the skill that should give them. Look at each PNG once. Never fix a colour or line weight here: the look is the standard's.

**What it shows.** Large (a detail area, 1:1,000 and larger): every building with its storeys (roman or arabic, as the standard's `storey_labels` says), entrances where the data has them, each an arrow into its door, the street surface, paths, trees as tree plans (a scalloped crown, its branches and trunk; a row of them along both sides of each street `streets/` draws as a centreline), hedges as bands with wavy sides, pools and playgrounds, and names, so a square reads as a place and not as a street: the squares, centres, parks and stops, the streets, and the buildings' special uses (school, daycare, pool); the ground floors open to the public hatched and the shared courtyards marked; at 1:1,000 and larger a ground-floor plan: the outer walls cut in black, open at the doors, the inside white, and each ground floor's use with its area where the layers give it (never a room or a flat the data doesn't hold), so the detail says what the site plan can't. Every plan names its squares, centres, parks and stops. The site plan (1:2,000 to 1:5,000): buildings, storeys if the brief asks, streets, green, trees as dots of their crown's size, hedges as a line, and water; on both, contour lines from the site folder's terrain model every metre, every fifth stronger with its height (`contour_m`), and without a terrain model, none, named in `drawings.json`; trees at every scale in three tones of the standard's green (`tree_tones`); the detail-area windows outlined, and the narrative's idea under the buildings in the accent's pale tone with its name, a line as a broad band, an area as a tint, so the plan carries what the panels promise. The site plan's legend is a bold heading and a list in two columns, each label with its sample lined up to its right, on a pale box with no outline over the plan's bottom-left corner, with no names under it; the other plans keep theirs in aligned columns under the map. Small (the figure-ground, 1:10,000 and smaller): buildings black on white and the site boundary, filling its panel frame where there is one, centred on the site. The new buildings carry each plan, white with an ink outline and a cast shadow; the accent's pale `public` tone marks the public ground: the massing's squares and mobility's shared streets.

**What to write**, into `plans/`: `site-plan_1-<scale>.svg` and `.png`, `detail-area-<n>_1-<scale>.svg` and `.png`, `figure-ground_1-<scale>.svg` and `.png`, `drawings.json`, and `summary.md` in three lines: each file with its scale on one line (`site-plan_1-3000.svg at 1:3,000 …`); how many of the brief's plans are drawn and fit the panel; what you are unsure of, such as a layer that was missing, what a detail area couldn't show, an idea no layer has as a shape, two detail areas that still overlap or are weak, a detail area too small for its subject, or a plan that had to be cropped.

# Site section

Reads: drawing-graphics, brief-reader, panel-layout
Reads (end): massing, open-space, structure-plan, narrative

Inputs: the project's site folder (the site polygon and its buildings, plots, streets, water and rail), the brief's checklist for the scales (where `panel-layout/layout.json` has frames for the cut and the excerpt, their scales, what their `shows` asks and their `file` names), the drawing standard for the look, and at the end `massing/massing.geojson`, `structure-plan/`, `open-space/` and `narrative/narrative.md`. Never invent data; if one is missing, say so in `summary.md`. Work in Python with `shapely`, `pyproj` and `requests`, in a metric projection, and write the SVG directly; make the PNG with a headless Chrome or Edge, giving it absolute paths. No Rhino.

**The section.** Run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/section.py" --site <site folder> --proposal <proposal> --scale <site plan scale> --detail-scale <largest scale> --style <proposal>/drawing-graphics/style.json`, and at the end again with `--massing`. It chooses the line itself (buildings, rail, main streets, water, the place you give with `--at`), takes the ground from the site folder's terrain model, else a terrain CSV, else a free elevation service, and says which in `profile.csv`. If the line it chose crosses nothing of interest, give your own with `--line` and say why in `summary.md`. The script runs the line 200 m past the site at each end (in a frame, as far as the frame is long), looks so that A is on your left, samples the ground every 10 m without vertical exaggeration, cuts the buildings on the line in the strongest tone and stands those up to 80 m behind in elevation on their own ground (where the site has 3D building models with roofs, it cuts the roofs along the line so pitched roofs read as pitched and draws those behind by their roof's outline, and a flat top at the measured height stands only where there is no model; give both counts, from `roofs` in `cut.json`, in `summary.md`), draws the ground behind the cut in bands from far to near so no building behind floats, and on the whole cut the landscape further back as ground lines about 300, 600 and 1,000 m behind, palest farthest, where the terrain reaches, puts trees, grass and people by land use, labels each street, railway and river once, marks the site boundary in the accent, and adds a scale bar, heights above sea level and a key plan. It draws the whole cut at the site plan scale and a 200 m excerpt with floor lines and people at the largest scale; with `--massing` the same on the design, on the same line, new buildings in the standard's `new` tone with an ink outline, and the trees of `massing/` and `open-space/` that reach the line or stand just behind it. If the brief asks for elevations, draw them the same way from the street.

**The design pass tells the story**, as the reference sections do: the areas of `structure-plan/` and `open-space/` as coloured bands in the earth, each named at its foot, people on open ground, and the narrative's principles as notes in the sky, each with a dot at its place and one dotted line through them all. Write `site-section/notes.json`, `[{"text": ..., "zone": ...}]`: each principle in the narrative's words, shortened, and the structure plan's or open space's area it is about, by its name (`zones` in `cut.json` lists those on the line), and pass `--notes` with it. A note whose area isn't on the line is spread along the site with a hollow dot, illustrative: name those in `summary.md`. Where the panels' plan (`panel-layout/layout-plan.json`, else `layout.json`) gives the cut or the excerpt a frame, or you give `--frame W,H` in mm, the drawing fills it and leaves the caption, scale bar and key plan to the panel; `assumptions.md` says when the frame is too low for the cut at its scale.

**The look.** Colours, line weights and fonts come from `drawing-graphics/standard.md`. Without it, black lines on white, greys for cut and elevation, and one accent for the site boundary and what is new. Open every PNG before you finish: labels that overlap, a ground line that is missing, or buildings that float are mistakes.

**What to write**, into `site-section/` in the proposal folder: `site-section_<scale>.svg` and `.png` for the whole cut, `site-section_excerpt_<scale>.svg` and `.png`, `profile.csv`, `cut.json`, `assumptions.md`, and `summary.md` in three lines. Write the scale in a file name as `1-2000`, and give each SVG its width and height in mm at its scale, so it prints true to scale. The summary's three lines: what you drew and at which scales, the height difference along the cut, what you are unsure of.

# Climate

Reads: pdf-to-md, site-kit
Reads (end): drawing-graphics, panel-layout

This skill describes the place, then says what that asks of the design. Read the brief's Markdown and pictures for climate or fresh air maps, traffic counts, speeds, noise studies and noise limits, and the project's site folder (`site.geojson`, buildings, streets, rail, plots). Work in the proposal folder you're given and write only into `climate/`. Never invent data: every number carries its source (brief page, dataset, year) or is named as an assumption, and what can't be backed is left out and named in `summary.md`. Each step is a script in `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/`, run as `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/<script>.py" --site <site folder> --out <proposal>/climate`; `--help` explains each. Needs `pip install shapely pyproj numpy requests pillow pymupdf tzdata`, and Chrome or Edge for the PNGs.

1. **Fresh air** (`fresh_air.py`). If the brief has a climate map: `page` extracts it; pick three or more street crossings you can see on the map and in reality (`crossing` gives their coordinates), `fit`, and open `fit-check.png`: the site's streets must lie on the map's streets, about 100 m off is normal for a small map. Read its legend (if the brief has none, say so). In `classes.json` give each corridor as `at_px`, a pixel in its strongest colour: pale tints of that colour around it are not corridor. Give the arrows as colour ranges with the way they point as you see it, `trace`, and open `trace-check.png`: the green outline must follow only the corridor band. A WARNING means the colour caught too much or nothing; pick again. Without a map, `derive` from terrain and say there is no study.
2. **Sun** (`sun.py`): sun positions, shadows at 9, 12 and 15 h on 21 March and 21 December, and annual sun hours and radiation from an EPW weather file, so clouds count. It takes an `.epw` from the site folder if there is one, else a typical year from PVGIS.
3. **Wind** (`wind.py`): ten years of hourly wind, as a rose for the year, winter and summer.
4. **Noise** (`noise.py`): write `noise-sources.json` from the brief: each road with its daily traffic, speed and class, or an emission level from a noise study, each with its source; leave out what has no numbers and name it. A road often changes name along the way: list every name it carries (`"name": ["A", "B"]`), then check on the map that the loud band follows the whole road. Where the brief gives a range, give it as a range (`"aadt": [low, high]`): the maps and rules take the high end, and `summary.md` gives the shares at both ends. A speed without a source is ASSUMED. Buildings screen the noise. Give the railway's trains per day from the brief, a study or the site folder, and if none has them look for a published count (parliament, ministry, rail operator, national noise map); put them in the sources file, or use `--rail-trains N --rail-source "..."`. The number is per line in the rail layer, so where it draws each track apart, give each its share. Make passenger and freight two sources (freight `disc_brake_pct` 0). With no number at all it stays off and the maps say so. Never assume train numbers outside a test, and mark a test value ASSUMED.
5. **Heat** (`heat.py`): a heat-island index from what covers the ground (roofs, roads, land use, trees, water) in the site folder; relative, not a temperature.
6. **Rules** (`rules.py`): put the brief's or the country's noise limits in `thresholds.json` with their source; without them it uses the German DIN 18005 and says so; the noise method (RLS-90, Schall 03) is German too, so on a site elsewhere say that in `summary.md`. It writes where not to build homes, where only behind a shielding edge, which corridors to keep open, which way to orient streets, and the wind notes. It also writes `climate.json`, the file for the design skills: the DON'T, CAREFUL and DO zones as GeoJSON polygons with the rule and its reason, and the key numbers.
7. **Drawings** (`draw.py`): the look comes from `drawing-graphics/` in the proposal folder (its `style.json`, else the colours and font named in `standard.md`), else black on white with one accent; check `drawings.txt` says which. The script draws every map to the maps' frame in `panel-layout/layout-plan.json`, else `layout.json` (its size, scale and centre, a short legend inside); without one, take the scale from the brief's checklist (`--scale`). Every map has a legend, north arrow, scale bar and sources. Open every PNG; fix what overlaps or reads wrong. On a second run, when `drawing-graphics/` now exists in the proposal folder, run only this step again (no recalculation) so every map and the sheet take the entry's colours; a panel then reuses them. After writing `summary.md`, run `draw.py --sheet` for `climate_sheet`: all maps on one A3 sheet with the summary.

Then write `climate.md`, one page: for each topic what it shows on this site and which parts it constrains, each line with its file or brief page, then the rules, then sources and licences (Open-Meteo CC BY 4.0, PVGIS © EU, OpenStreetMap ODbL). And `summary.md`, three lines: what you made, the one number that matters most (such as the share of the site too loud for homes), what you are least sure of. To check a design, run `sun.py` and `noise.py` again with `--buildings <its buildings>` into `climate/design/`.

# Site kit

Reads: nothing

Never hard-code a site, a city or a bounding box in this skill or in a script it makes; take the name, the stated area and the maps from the brief you are given. Never invent data. If a layer can't be found, leave it out and say so in `summary.md`.

**Where to look.** Collect the project site plus a margin wide enough for the smallest-scale drawing the brief asks for: a figure-ground at 1:15,000 on a 30 cm square needs about 2 km on every side; otherwise about 600 m. Go further if the brief names neighbours that lie further out, such as a station or a commercial area. Use OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API (`https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter`, try a mirror if it is busy) for buildings, streets, landuse, water and rail. For heights, try the state's open 3D building data (in Bavaria LoD2, in Thuringia LoD2 from GDI-Th) first, then `height` and `building:levels` tags in OSM. Where neither exists, use a stated default per building type (for example 2 floors for houses, 1 for halls) and flag it in the data with `height_source`. For the street land, try the open cadastre or land-use map (in Germany the state's ALKIS actual land use, with its streets, squares and paths as areas; elsewhere often the INSPIRE cadastral parcels, where the street is the land no plot covers).

**Finding the boundary.** If the brief gives a polygon or coordinates, use them. If it only shows the site on a map, render that page, locate the area on OpenStreetMap (match rail lines, main roads, forest edges and settlement edges), fit the map to coordinates, trace the marked outline and snap it to roads, rail or field edges where it follows them. Then check the area against any figure in the brief. State how close it is and how sure you are; a traced boundary is rarely better than 30 to 50 m.

**What to write.** Everything into the project's site folder: the one you're told, else where the project's `CLAUDE.md` says, else `site/` at the top. The site belongs to the project, not to one version, so every version reads the same data. If the folder already has a `site.geojson`, ask before you replace it.

- `site.geojson`: one polygon, WGS84, longitude first, `kind: "site"`.
- `buildings.geojson`: `height`, `floors`, `use`, `height_source`.
- `buildings-3d.geojson`, when the 3D building data has roofs: every wall and roof surface as a polygon with x, y and z, z in metres above the building's lowest ground point, with the building's `id` and `surface` (`wall` or `roof`).
- `plots.geojson`: `landuse` (OSM landuse, natural and leisure polygons).
- `streets.geojson`, `water.geojson`, `rail.geojson`: lines, with names and types where known.
- `street-land.geojson`, if the cadastre has it: polygons, `use` street, square or path, `name`, `source`.
- `kit.json`: `label`, `center`, `bbox` (west, south, east, north), `size_m`, `generated`.
- `SOURCES.md`: each file, its source and licence (OSM is ODbL), the attribution line, and every default you applied.
- `summary.md`: three lines. What you collected, the site area in ha, what you are unsure of.

# PDF to Markdown

Reads: nothing, only the PDFs in the project

Much of what a project needs comes as PDF: the brief, a development plan, a traffic or noise study, city statistics, a reference project. The other skills read text. This skill converts each PDF with Docling, which keeps headings, lists and tables in reading order, so a number in a table stays next to its label. A marker `<!-- page N -->` stands before each page, so whoever takes a number from it can cite the file and the page.

Convert the PDFs the user names, or else every PDF in the project that has no Markdown yet. Write each result next to its PDF, so every version of a proposal reads the same text. For each: `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/pdf_to_md.py" <pdf> <the PDF's folder>/ --images`. Add `--ocr` only if a page comes out empty but has text in the PDF, a scan. It writes `<name>.md` and the pictures (maps, plans, drawings, photos) at 300 dpi to `<name>-images/`, named by page, leaving out icons and logos under 3 cm. Plans and maps drawn in vectors also go to `<name>-drawings/` with the legend beside them, as PDF, SVG and PNG (`pip install pymupdf`). The first run downloads Docling's models, about 500 MB. If Docling isn't installed: `pip install docling`.

Then read each result against its PDF on a few pages with tables or key numbers. Fix nothing by hand. Next to each, write `<name>-summary.md`, one page at most, from its Markdown: what the document is and from whom, then what matters most in it (the task, key numbers and areas, dates, what it requires), each line with its page `(p. N)`. Only what it says; add nothing. Keep an `index.md` in the same folder, one line per PDF: where it came from, what it is, its pages. Write `summary.md` next to it, in three lines: which PDFs were converted, how many pages and tables, and any page that came out wrong or empty.
